text: [Music]
Maximizing your time isn't about
cramming more into your day. It's about
being deliberate. It's about figuring
out what will matter a month from now, a
year from now, even a decade from now,
and scheduling time for it this week.
When Friday afternoon rolls around and I
feel like my week was largely a waste of
time, it's almost always because I just
reacted to incoming requests and did my
same old tasks. That kind of week
doesn't build the kind of life I want.
And I doubt it builds the kind you want
either. So, let's change that. Let's be
intentional and optimize the time we've
got. Here are five habits that will
help. Time optimization habit number
one, the weekly big four.
Kick off your week by thinking of the
four areas that will make your life
bigger, better, and richer. Promises,
people, personal enjoyment, and profit.
Set up a simple cananband board with a
column for each category. I use Trello
to build my canban boards, but I know
many people who use Notion. Spend 15
minutes on Sunday night or Monday
morning populating each column with
things you can do during the week. In
column number one, add any projects you
promised others that you want to knock
out of the park. like a pitch deck you
promised your boss you'd deliver or that
video you promised your YouTube
subscribers. When you overd deliver and
exceed people's expectations, bigger and
better career opportunities come your
way. If you run a business, exceeding
expectations means loyal customers and
more business through word of
mouth. In column two, the people column,
list a handful of special things you can
do for the people you care about most.
Start with the people you would want by
your side at your
deathbed. For example, plan a surprise
date night with your wife or reserve an
hour to help your son with his school
project. In the personal enjoyment
column, list activities you could
schedule this week that you can get
excited about, like a round of golf with
a great friend, a games night with
friends, or time to go hiking while
listening to a new audio book.
In the profit column, list a few things
you can do this week that will allow you
to earn more money a year from now. Like
get a testimonial from a satisfied
customer to drive more sales or read I
will teach you to be rich and learn two
powerful strategies to secure a raise in
months. Once you've thought of items for
each column, ask what one thing can I do
in each column to make my week
meaningful and memorable?
Block out time in your calendar for each
item. It doesn't have to be a lot of
time, maybe just 15 minutes. The key is
that you do something this week to move
the needle on what will truly matter
over the course of your
life. Time optimization habit number
two. Capture and
interrogate. The first objective each
day is to eliminate overwhelm. So, grab
a coffee, tea, or glass of water, and
write down everything you feel you need
to get done today on a fresh notebook
page, blank sheet of paper, or new
document on your computer. Now, it's
time to interrogate the list and find
which are essential. Start by accepting
that none of the items on your list get
done. That's right. Not a single thing
you want to do gets done today. Now,
item by item, ask yourself, what's the
fallout for not doing this item? Fast
forward one month and try to imagine the
consequences. Feel the pain, the
personal backlash, or the regret of
missing a great
opportunity. You'll find most tasks come
with little to no consequence. You
missed a meeting that didn't matter. You
skipped a task that had no real impact
on a project. Life moved on, and so did
everyone
else. But there are a critical few tasks
with intolerable consequences. Not
following through on a promise to your
manager could permanently damage their
trust in you. Missing that client
deadline might cost your company the
account and jeopardize a promotion for
the next year. Skipping your child's
championship game, which they've talked
about for weeks, creates a memory of
your absence they'll carry for
years. On a scale from 0 to 100, where
zero means it makes no difference, and
100 means it would be completely
unacceptable to let it slide, rate every
item on your day's to-do list. Anything
you rate above 90 is an excellent use of
your time today. For everything else,
either ask someone else to do,
deliberately postpone, or accept the
small discomfort of never doing. By
choosing fewer, more meaningful tasks
and giving them your full attention,
you'll get more done and be
significantly happier with how you spend
your
time. Time optimization habit number
three, the prioritizing thought
experiment.
When you need to pinpoint your true
priority for the day and attack it
immediately, conduct this powerful
thought
experiment. Imagine your phone rings.
It's your closest friend or family
member who urgently needs your help in
an hour and they'll need you for the
rest of the day. You can't say no.
Therefore, in 1 hour, you must abandon
all your work plans. If you expected to
do 8 hours of work today, you now just
have 60 minutes to be
productive. What do you do?
This mental scenario forces your genuine
priority to emerge fast. Your attention
might go to that report, email, or
client pitch you wanted to get done, so
you immediately get to work on it. Or if
you vowed that you would exercise today,
you immediately lace up your running
shoes and head
outside. I use this mental hack
throughout the day to reset my focus. It
dramatically eliminates timewasting
activities and concentrates my focus on
what truly matters.
Time optimization habit number four,
dedicated
days. Complete this statement. The
better I do, blank, the more likely I'll
succeed in my current
role. Of all your responsibilities at
work, there are less than five things
that if done well determine more than
80% of your
success. For me, it's writing and
recording video scripts, animating
videos, creating great products, and
selling those products.
If I get better at those, my business
grows. If I stop improving in those
areas, my business
fails. Out of school, working as a
junior engineer, more than 80% of my
promotion depended on understanding
design standards and mastering a
software program called AutoCAD. I got
promoted to bigger roles because I
steadily improved in those
areas. Identify the few things you need
to do well to thrive in your job. Then
dedicate at least one day a week to
mainly doing one of those things or
getting better at it. For example, I
dedicate Monday to animation, Tuesday
and Wednesday to writing and recording,
Thursday to new products, Friday to
sales. The beauty of this method is that
I can stay in one mode for most of the
day and don't need to constantly switch
between responsibilities. As a result, I
get more done.
If you can't block off entire days to
focus on a responsibility, simply use
any downtime to focus on the theme of
the day. For instance, dedicate specific
days to mastering that essential
software program your company relies on,
and use those 15-minute gaps between
meetings or projects to learn advanced
techniques that will set you apart from
your peers.
When you theme your days around a vital
responsibility at work, it becomes the
first thing on your mind that day and
you're constantly looking for
opportunities to practice it, which
ensures you spend more time on things
that truly
matter. Time optimization habit number
five, the hell yeah filter. Your
response to every project proposal or
social event request should be hell yeah
or sorry, I'm too busy right now. If you
commit to too many mildly interesting
things, you'll quickly feel
overcommitted. What seem like
opportunities will become
obligations. You'll wake up most
mornings wondering, "Why did I say yes
to this?" A great way to determine if a
request is a hell yeah is to ask
yourself, "If I had to do this thing
tomorrow, would I be excited enough to
make time for it?" It's easy to agree to
future commitments we only somewhat want
to do, then dread them when the day
arrives. The hell yeah filter keeps your
calendar filled with only what truly
matters to
you. Those were the top five time
optimization habits that I've adopted
over the last decade. If you would like
